sub.name: Development of ideas

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: T4 fairly presses optionality as a possible excuse for doing nothing.
sub.limitation: T7 misreads the Strategist as 'always tied to high stress'; T6 said train on easy days.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: T3 argues a fixed schedule is fragile because it 'shatters at the first' shift change.
sub.limitation: T2's 'mechanical life' objection to triggers is rhetorical, not tested.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: Clear's never-miss-twice and Camus's indifferent world are attributed fairly.
sub.limitation: T6 'gain fitness from recovery after high stress' stretches Taleb into training advice.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: T5 hedges: 'It is possible you fear the lack of structure.'
sub.limitation: T1 'You must' and T6's flat prescriptions state preferences as facts.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: T8 says 'My previous stance was too focused on acceptance.'
sub.limitation: T6 never answers T4's charge that optionality becomes an excuse.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: T1 says the problem is motivation tied to a time the schedule makes impossible.
sub.limitation: Doesn't ask why the user 'keeps giving up': energy, time, or guilt.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: T6 uses shift difficulty to set workout intensity.
sub.limitation: Nothing on night shifts, sleep or commute, which shape a shift worker's options.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: T9 makes the user choose between steady habit and resilience.
sub.limitation: The user asked for a routine; the speakers impose identity versus antifragility.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: T6 'On a brutal shift day, do nothing.'
sub.limitation: Shift-work fatigue and recovery appear only in Section E.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: Section E gives conditional branches by priority.
sub.limitation: No focused questions about the shift pattern or past failures.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: T9 contrasts the comfort of a steady habit with resilience.
sub.limitation: Desires are the speakers' categories; the user's reasons to exercise are never explored.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: T6 challenges the idea that consistency means 'a flat, consistent line.'
sub.limitation: The all-or-nothing assumption behind giving up isn't named.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: Section E: mental comfort versus overall fitness and resilience.
sub.limitation: The fitness-vs-comfort framing is asserted, not drawn from the user.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: T5 says the frustration stems from feeling a lack of control and from self-judgment.
sub.limitation: No look at outside pressure or shame about repeated failure.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: T9: 'The user must decide' which they value.
sub.limitation: Offers a binary choice rather than distinctions the user can refine.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: Section E sets tiny triggers against an opportunistic model.
sub.limitation: No hybrid or minimal-step option, despite T7's micro-habit.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: T7: volatility risks losing the identity of someone who exercises.
sub.limitation: The cost of fixed triggers on exhausting days is never weighed.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: Section E: if steady habit matters for mental comfort, adopt tiny triggers.
sub.limitation: Conditions depend on abstract priorities, not observable facts about the shifts.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: Section A names the comfort-versus-resilience uncertainty.
sub.limitation: Major unknowns like energy, sleep and equipment go unseparated.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: Section E: try both methods for two weeks.
sub.limitation: Tracking 'recovery time' is a vague measure for a habit question.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: T1's front-door trigger is plain and concrete.
sub.limitation: T3 'optionality' and 'fragility trap' need unpacking.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: T9 restates who wants what clearly.
sub.limitation: T7 'that approach' points to a misread version of T6.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: Nine turns, all within 25 to 65 words.
sub.limitation: T9 runs long with recap.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: The three lenses (habit, absurd, antifragile) stay distinct.
sub.limitation: The T8 shift is explicit but blurs the Existentialist into the Habitualist.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: Turns are tight, with little filler.
sub.limitation: Section D partly repeats T9.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: T7 frames identity itself at stake.
sub.limitation: Tension stays conceptual, not tied to a lived moment.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: T8 Existentialist reverses toward chosen identity.
sub.limitation: The reversal comes with no pressure that earns it.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: T2's Camus voice: schedule 'does not care about your routine.'
sub.limitation: The Habitualist's voice is generic coaching.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: T2 pictures the rock rolling back down each time the shift changes.
sub.limitation: Few other images beyond Sisyphus.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: T5 moves from defeat to joy in movement.
sub.limitation: The rhythm is flat; every turn has the same weight.

strengths: Three clearly distinct lenses, with T2's Sisyphus image making the frustration vivid
T6 to T7 surfaces a real tension: adaptive intensity versus a stable exercise identity
T5 names fear and self-judgment in hedged terms
weaknesses: T7 Habitualist misreads T6 as exercise 'always tied to high stress'
T4 never-miss-twice versus T6 'do nothing' left unresolved and unanswered
No questions about the shift pattern; Section E's 'recovery time' test is vague
editorNotes: Require a speaker to restate the opponent's claim before rebutting it, to stop misreads like T7.
Require one turn or Section E to ask two focused questions about the user's shift pattern and energy.
Require Section E's test to measure the behaviour in question, such as sessions done, not proxies.
